statement: If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.
heath_proof: For let the number A have its half odd; I say that A is even-times odd only. Now that it is even-times odd is manifest; for the half of it, being odd, measures it an even number of times. [VII. Def. 9] I say next that it is also even-times odd only. For, if A is even-times even also, it will be measured by an even number according to an even number; [VII. Def. 8] so that the half of it will also be measured by an even number though it is odd: which is absurd. Therefore A is even-times odd only.

**Statement:** If a number have its half odd, it is even-times odd only.

**Step 1.** Let N be a number whose half is odd. Then N = 2C for some odd number C. Since N is divided into two equal parts, N is even [D7.6].

**Step 2.** Now, 2 is even [D7.6] and C is odd, so N is measured by the even number 2 according to the odd number C. Therefore N is even-times odd [D7.9].

**Step 3.** It remains to show that N is even-times odd only, that is, N is not also even-times even and not odd-times odd.

**Step 4.** Suppose for contradiction that N is even-times even. Then by definition [D7.8], N is measured by some even number A according to some even number B, so that N = A times B with both A and B even.

**Step 5.** Since A is even, A is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6], so A = 2m for some number m. Then N = 2m times B, and therefore the half of N is m times B.

**Step 6.** Since B is even, B is divisible into two equal parts [D7.6], so B = 2n for some number n. Then m times B = m times 2n = 2 times (m times n), so m times B is divisible into two equal parts, namely m times n and m times n. Therefore m times B is even [D7.6].

**Step 7.** But the half of N is C, which is odd. Since a number cannot be both even and odd [D7.6, D7.7], this is a contradiction. Therefore N is not even-times even.

**Step 8.** Now suppose for contradiction that N is odd-times odd. Then by definition [D7.10], N is measured by some odd number P according to some odd number Q, so that N = P times Q with both P and Q odd.

**Step 9.** But if an odd number multiplies an odd number, the product is odd [9.29]. Therefore N = P times Q is odd.

**Step 10.** However, N is even (Step 1). Since a number cannot be both even and odd [D7.6, D7.7], this is a contradiction. Therefore N is not odd-times odd.

**Step 11.** Since N is even-times odd (Step 2), and N is neither even-times even (Step 7) nor odd-times odd (Step 10), N is even-times odd only. Q.E.D.
